entries.meaning: Bored and no longer excited, after too much of something. ---
examples: After twenty years in the business he is pretty jaded.
Jaded voters stayed home on election day.
She was jaded about dating apps long before she quit them.

entries.meaning: Having a rough, uneven edge with sharp points. ---
examples: He cut his foot on a jagged piece of glass.
The coastline here is rocky and jagged.
A jagged line ran down the middle of the screen.
entries.contrast: The -ed is a full syllable — JAG-id, not jagd.

entries.meaning: Completely full of people or things. ---
examples: The stadium was jam-packed an hour before kickoff.
The book is jam-packed with photographs.
We rode a jam-packed subway car to the game.

entries.meaning: From Jamaica, or belonging to it. ---
examples: Jamaican coffee is expensive for a reason.
The restaurant serves Jamaican food.
Her mother is Jamaican.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the person: she's a Jamaican.

entries.meaning: Jammed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The copier is jammed again.
He could not get the jammed window open.
The highway was jammed with traffic.
We squeezed into a jammed elevator.

senses.head: Stuck so that it will not move or work
examples: The copier is jammed again.
He could not get the jammed window open.

senses.head: Filled with too many people or things
examples: The highway was jammed with traffic.
We squeezed into a jammed elevator.

entries.takes: with + noun, in the crowded sense

entries.meaning: Unpleasantly surprising because it does not fit. ---
examples: The ending was jarring.
There is a jarring shift in tone halfway through the book.
It is jarring to hear your own voice recorded.
entries.form: -ing from jar — to give an unpleasant shock

entries.meaning: Jaundiced has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He takes a jaundiced view of campaign promises.
She looked at the new plan with a jaundiced eye.
The newborn was slightly jaundiced for a few days.
His skin looked jaundiced under the lamp.

senses.head: Seeing things bitterly and suspiciously after bad experience
examples: He takes a jaundiced view of campaign promises.
She looked at the new plan with a jaundiced eye.

senses.head: Having yellow skin and eyes because of liver trouble
examples: The newborn was slightly jaundiced for a few days.
His skin looked jaundiced under the lamp.

entries.position: both — the figurative sense almost always before a noun

entries.meaning: Cheerful and confident in a lively, stylish way. ---
examples: He wore his hat at a jaunty angle.
She came in with a jaunty step.
His mood was jauntier than it had been all week.

entries.meaning: Jazzy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The soundtrack has a jazzy feel.
They played a jazzy version of the old hymn.
He showed up in a jazzy orange tie.
The new logo is a lot jazzier than the old one.

senses.head: Sounding like jazz
examples: The soundtrack has a jazzy feel.
They played a jazzy version of the old hymn.

senses.head: Bright and showy
examples: He showed up in a jazzy orange tie.
The new logo is a lot jazzier than the old one.

entries.meaning: Belonging to Thomas Jefferson's ideas of limited government and independent citizens. ---
examples: He appealed to Jeffersonian ideals of small government.
Jeffersonian democracy rested on the independent farmer.
The essay traces the Jeffersonian strain in American politics.

entries.meaning: Moving in sudden, uneven starts and stops. ---
examples: The camera work is jerky and hard to watch.
The old elevator starts with a jerky motion.
His movements got jerkier as he tired.
entries.contrast: Also a noun, the dried meat: beef jerky.

entries.meaning: Deep, shiny black. ---
examples: She has jet-black hair.
The horse was jet-black except for one white foot.
He drives a jet-black pickup.
entries.form: compound — jet, a black stone, + black

entries.meaning: Decorated with jewels. ---
examples: She wore a jeweled bracelet.
The crown has a jeweled cross on top.
A jeweled dagger sat in the display case.
entries.contrast: American spelling has one l; British writing has jewelled.

entries.meaning: Belonging to armed Islamist groups that call their fight a holy war. ---
examples: The group ran a network of jihadi websites.
He was tried on charges of jihadi recruitment.
Jihadi propaganda spread through the app.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the person, and also written jihadist.

entries.meaning: Suddenly left by a lover or a fiancé. ---
examples: The story is told by a jilted bride.
A jilted boyfriend keyed her car.
He plays the jilted lover in the second act.

entries.meaning: Loudly patriotic in an aggressive way toward other countries. ---
examples: The coverage turned jingoistic once the war started.
He gave a jingoistic speech about national greatness.
Critics called the movie jingoistic.

entries.meaning: Seeming to bring bad luck, or to have it. ---
examples: That car is jinxed — it has broken down four times.
I felt jinxed after losing three games in a row.
The whole project seemed jinxed from the start.

entries.meaning: Nervous and unable to keep still. ---
examples: Three cups of coffee made me jittery.
Investors are jittery about the election.
She gets jittery before a presentation.

entries.meaning: Without paid work. ---
examples: He has been jobless since the plant closed.
Jobless claims fell again last month.
Thousands of workers were left jobless.
entries.contrast: Jobless is the newspaper word and also describes figures (jobless claims); unemployed is the more formal one for a person.

entries.meaning: Done, owned or shared by two or more people or groups. ---
examples: They filed a joint tax return.
The two countries issued a joint statement.
It was a joint effort by three departments.
entries.contrast: Also a common noun: a knee joint, and informally a place — a pizza joint.

entries.meaning: From Jordan, or belonging to it. ---
examples: The Jordanian government denied the report.
We met a Jordanian student at the conference.
Her husband is Jordanian.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the person: two Jordanians were on the flight.

entries.meaning: Having to do with the work of reporters and news writing. ---
examples: The piece fails basic journalistic standards.
She won the prize for journalistic integrity.
Journalistic sources are protected by law in most states.

entries.meaning: Cheerful and friendly, often loudly so. ---
examples: Our host was loud and jovial.
He was in a jovial mood all evening.
A jovial man in a red sweater handed out cider.

entries.meaning: Full of happiness, or showing it. ---
examples: It was a joyful reunion.
The choir sang a joyful hymn.
Everyone looked joyful when the news came through.

entries.meaning: Giving or showing no pleasure at all. ---
examples: It was a joyless meal in a silent kitchen.
The work became joyless after the reorganization.
She described her childhood as joyless.

entries.meaning: Full of great happiness. ---
examples: It was a joyous occasion for the whole family.
The crowd let out a joyous shout.
The entire weekend was joyous.
entries.contrast: Formal or literary; in ordinary speech Americans say joyful or just happy.

entries.meaning: Openly delighted, usually after a win or good news. ---
examples: Jubilant fans poured onto the field.
She was jubilant after the verdict.
A jubilant crowd filled the square until midnight.

entries.meaning: Shared by the Jewish and Christian traditions. ---
examples: He appealed to Judeo-Christian values.
The course covers the Judeo-Christian tradition.
Judeo-Christian ethics shaped the law of that period.

entries.meaning: Too quick to criticize other people. ---
examples: I do not want to sound judgmental, but that was a mistake.
She is judgmental about how other people raise their kids.
He gave me a judgmental look over his glasses.
entries.contrast: American spelling drops the e: judgmental, judgment.

entries.meaning: Having to do with courts, judges and the law. ---
examples: The law faces judicial review in the fall.
Judicial appointments to that court are for life.
She built her career in the judicial branch.
entries.contrast: Judicial means "of the courts"; judicious means "showing good judgment".

entries.meaning: Showing good sense and careful judgment. ---
examples: A judicious use of salt makes all the difference.
He was judicious about what he said in public.
The editor made a few judicious cuts.
entries.contrast: Not the same word as judicial, which is about courts.

entries.meaning: Juicy has 2 distinct senses.
examples: These peaches are juicy.
This one is juicier than the last.
She has all the juicy details.
The book is full of juicy stories about the studio.

senses.head: Full of juice
examples: These peaches are juicy.
This one is juicier than the last.

senses.head: Interesting because it is scandalous or full of gossip
examples: She has all the juicy details.
The book is full of juicy stories about the studio.

entries.meaning: Mixed together with no order. ---
examples: The papers were jumbled in a cardboard box.
Her notes are a jumbled mess.
My memory of that night is jumbled.

entries.meaning: Much bigger than the usual size, especially of a product. ---
examples: She ordered a jumbo box of popcorn.
Jumbo shrimp cost more per pound.
The store sells eggs in a jumbo size.

entries.meaning: Nervous and easily startled. ---
examples: The dog is jumpy around strangers.
I have been jumpy ever since the break-in.
He gets jumpier the closer we get to the deadline.

entries.meaning: Lower in rank, or younger. ---
examples: She is a junior partner at the firm.
Two junior staffers wrote the report.
He is junior to me by three years.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a junior in high school, she's the junior on the team.

entries.meaning: Put together quickly from whatever was on hand. ---
examples: They sailed home under a jury-rigged mast.
The whole setup is jury-rigged with duct tape.
He built a jury-rigged antenna out of a coat hanger.
entries.form: compound — noun + participle, from sailing, where a jury mast was a temporary one
entries.contrast: Often mixed up with jerry-built, which means badly built rather than temporary.

entries.meaning: Fair and morally right. ---
examples: It was a just decision.
They spent their lives fighting for a just society.
The punishment seemed just to everyone in the room.
entries.contrast: The adjective means "fair". The everyday just in I just got here is an adverb and a different use altogether.

entries.meaning: Able to be defended as reasonable or right. ---
examples: The expense is justifiable given the results.
The court ruled it was justifiable self-defense.
Her anger was entirely justifiable.

entries.meaning: Justified has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her complaint was fully justified.
You were justified in walking out of that meeting.
The columns are justified on both sides.
Set the paragraph to justified rather than ragged right.

senses.head: Having a good reason; fair in the circumstances
examples: Her complaint was fully justified.
You were justified in walking out of that meeting.

senses.head: Of text, spaced so that both margins line up evenly
examples: The columns are justified on both sides.
Set the paragraph to justified rather than ragged right.

entries.meaning: Juvenile has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The case went to juvenile court.
Juvenile crime dropped sharply in the 1990s.
His jokes are juvenile.
Stop being so juvenile about it.

senses.head: Having to do with young people below the legal adult age
examples: The case went to juvenile court.
Juvenile crime dropped sharply in the 1990s.

senses.head: Childish in a way that annoys adults
examples: His jokes are juvenile.
Stop being so juvenile about it.

entries.contrast: Also a noun in legal and news writing: a juvenile was arrested.

entries.meaning: Placed side by side so that the difference shows. ---
examples: The two photographs are juxtaposed on facing pages.
The juxtaposed images make the point better than any caption.
Her calm voice, juxtaposed with the sirens, was eerie.

entries.meaning: Nightmarishly confusing and impersonal, like the bureaucracy in Kafka's novels. ---
examples: Getting the permit was a Kafkaesque ordeal.
The whole appeals process felt Kafkaesque.
He describes a Kafkaesque maze of forms and phone trees.

entries.meaning: Made of many bright parts that keep shifting. ---
examples: The film offers a kaleidoscopic view of the city.
Sunlight through the glass made a kaleidoscopic pattern on the floor.
Her novels are kaleidoscopic — dozens of voices at once.

entries.meaning: Broken and finished, beyond repair. ---
examples: The washing machine is kaput.
My old laptop finally went kaput.
After the storm the generator was kaput.
entries.position: predicative only — after a verb: the TV is kaput, never a kaput TV
entries.contrast: Informal and a little jokey; in writing use broken or out of order.

entries.meaning: From Kashmir, or belonging to it. ---
examples: She bought a Kashmiri shawl.
Kashmiri cooking uses a lot of saffron.
His grandparents were Kashmiri.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the person and for the language.

entries.meaning: From Kenya, or belonging to it. ---
examples: The Kenyan runners swept the race.
We had Kenyan coffee at breakfast.
Her father is Kenyan.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the person: three Kenyans finished in the top ten.

entries.meaning: Most important; the one the rest depends on. ---
examples: She played a key role in the negotiations.
Key witnesses refused to testify.
Timing is key to the whole plan.
entries.contrast: Also a very common noun: house keys, the key to the puzzle.

entries.meaning: Working without a physical key. ---
examples: The car has keyless entry.
Our front door uses a keyless lock.
Keyless ignition became standard on that model.

entries.meaning: Following Keynes's idea that government spending should support demand. ---
examples: The stimulus was a classic Keynesian response.
He teaches Keynesian economics.
Keynesian policy favors spending in a downturn.
entries.contrast: Said KAYN-, not KEEN-, because the name Keynes rhymes with rains.

entries.meaning: Of a dull yellowish-brown color. ---
examples: He wore a khaki jacket.
The uniform was khaki with brown boots.
She bought two pairs of khaki pants.
entries.contrast: Also a noun; the plural khakis means the pants themselves.

entries.meaning: Naturally kind and generous toward others. ---
examples: She is the most kindhearted person I know.
He was a gruff but kindhearted old man.
A kindhearted neighbor shoveled our walk.

entries.meaning: Kind and gentle in manner. ---
examples: A kindly woman showed us the way to the station.
He had a kindly face and a slow way of talking.
She was kindlier to strangers than to her own family.
entries.contrast: Kindly is far more common as an adverb (kindly step back); as an adjective it is slightly old-fashioned and usually sits before a noun.

entries.meaning: Of the same kind, or feeling the same way. ---
examples: We were kindred spirits from the first conversation.
The two languages are kindred tongues.
They share a kindred interest in old maps.
entries.contrast: Nearly always in the fixed phrase a kindred spirit, meaning someone who thinks and feels as you do.

entries.meaning: Kinetic has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed.
The museum has a room of kinetic sculpture.
The dance number is wildly kinetic.
His prose has a kinetic rhythm to it.

senses.head: Having to do with movement, especially in physics
examples: Kinetic energy depends on mass and speed.
The museum has a room of kinetic sculpture.

senses.head: Full of fast, restless energy
examples: The dance number is wildly kinetic.
His prose has a kinetic rhythm to it.

entries.meaning: Of the largest size made, especially of a bed. ---
examples: We slept in a king-size bed.
He bought a king-size candy bar.
The room comes with a king-size mattress.
entries.contrast: Also written king-sized; both are normal in American English.

entries.meaning: Kinky has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The novel has a kinky streak running through it.
He had some kinky ideas about the costume party.
Her hair is thick and kinky.
The cord got kinkier every time we coiled it.

senses.head: Involving unusual sexual tastes
examples: The novel has a kinky streak running through it.
He had some kinky ideas about the costume party.

senses.head: Of hair, wire or cord, full of tight curls or bends
examples: Her hair is thick and kinky.
The cord got kinkier every time we coiled it.

entries.contrast: The sexual meaning is the one most listeners hear first, so kinky hair can sound like a joke; many Americans say coily or tightly curled instead.

entries.meaning: Cheap and tasteless, often in a way people enjoy on purpose. ---
examples: The lobby is full of kitschy souvenirs.
I love how kitschy that diner is.
Their decorations get kitschier every Christmas.

entries.meaning: Knee-deep has 2 distinct senses.
examples: We waded through knee-deep water.
The snow was knee-deep by morning.
He is knee-deep in paperwork.
By then she was knee-deep in the investigation.

senses.head: Deep enough to reach the knees
examples: We waded through knee-deep water.
The snow was knee-deep by morning.

senses.head: Deeply involved in something, usually work or trouble
examples: He is knee-deep in paperwork.
By then she was knee-deep in the investigation.

entries.meaning: Long enough to reach the knee. ---
examples: She wore a knee-length skirt.
Knee-length boots are back in style.
The coat is knee-length.

entries.meaning: Made by knitting yarn. ---
examples: She gave me a knitted scarf.
He pulled on a knitted hat.
The store sells knitted blankets.
entries.contrast: Knit works as the adjective too, and is more common in short phrases: a knit cap.

entries.meaning: Covered with small round lumps. ---
examples: The old tree has knobby roots.
He had knobby knees and long arms.
These tires are knobbier than the ones made for pavement.

entries.meaning: Able to be known or found out. ---
examples: Some things are simply not knowable.
The exact number is not knowable from the records we have.
He wanted a knowable answer, not a guess.

entries.meaning: Showing that you understand something others have not said out loud. ---
examples: She gave me a knowing smile.
There was a knowing look between the two of them.
He answered with a knowing nod.
entries.contrast: A knowing look means the person is in on a secret; it does not mean "well informed" — that is knowledgeable.

entries.meaning: Knowing a lot about something. ---
examples: The salesperson was very knowledgeable about bikes.
We need a knowledgeable guide for the canyon.
She is the most knowledgeable person on the team.

entries.meaning: Recognized or established as a fact. ---
examples: He is a known troublemaker in the building.
The side effects are a known risk.
There is no known cure.
entries.contrast: Before a noun it means "recognized, on record": a known problem. After a verb, known as and known for are the passive verb, not this adjective.

entries.meaning: Strange in a harmless, funny way. ---
examples: She has a kooky sense of humor.
The neighbors are friendly but a little kooky.
His theories get kookier every year.

entries.meaning: Kosher has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The deli is strictly kosher.
We bought kosher salt for the recipe.
Something about the deal did not seem kosher.
Is it kosher to email him directly?

senses.head: Prepared according to Jewish dietary law
examples: The deli is strictly kosher.
We bought kosher salt for the recipe.

senses.head: Honest and above board
examples: Something about the deal did not seem kosher.
Is it kosher to email him directly?

entries.meaning: Belonging to the Kurds or their region. ---
examples: Kurdish forces held the north of the country.
He comes from a Kurdish family.
The village is mostly Kurdish.
entries.contrast: Also the name of the language: he speaks Kurdish.

entries.meaning: From Kuwait, or belonging to it. ---
examples: The Kuwaiti government funded the hospital.
He works for a Kuwaiti oil company.
Her business partner is Kuwaiti.
entries.contrast: Also a noun for the person: two Kuwaitis signed the deal.

entries.meaning: Marked with a label saying what it is. ---
examples: Every box was clearly labeled.
Keep the leftovers in a labeled container.
The wires were not labeled, so we had to guess.
entries.contrast: American spelling has one l; British writing has labelled.

entries.meaning: Needing a lot of人 work by hand. ---
examples: Picking the fruit by hand is labor-intensive.
It is a labor-intensive process that cannot be automated.
The new method is less labor-intensive than the old one.
entries.contrast: American spelling labor; British writing has labour-intensive.

entries.meaning: Labored has 2 distinct senses.
examples: His breathing was labored.
She climbed the last flight with labored steps.
The joke felt labored.
The essay ends on a labored note.

senses.head: Slow and difficult, especially of breathing or movement
examples: His breathing was labored.
She climbed the last flight with labored steps.

senses.head: Sounding forced instead of natural
examples: The joke felt labored.
The essay ends on a labored note.

entries.contrast: American spelling labored; British writing has laboured.

entries.meaning: Taking a lot of time and hard, dull effort. ---
examples: Copying the records by hand was laborious.
It is a laborious process, but it works.
He described the laborious business of restoring the piano.

entries.meaning: So complicated that it is hard to follow or to find your way through. ---
examples: The tax code is labyrinthine, even for accountants.
We got lost in the labyrinthine hallways of the old hospital.
Her novels have labyrinthine plots that reward a second reading.

entries.meaning: Laced has 2 distinct senses.
examples: The punch was laced with rum.
Police said the pills were laced with fentanyl.
His apology was laced with sarcasm.
He pulled on a pair of heavy laced boots.
The dress has a laced back that ties at the waist.

senses.head: Mixed with a small amount of alcohol, a drug or something else strong
examples: The punch was laced with rum.
Police said the pills were laced with fentanyl.
His apology was laced with sarcasm.

senses.head: Fastened or trimmed with laces
examples: He pulled on a pair of heavy laced boots.
The dress has a laced back that ties at the waist.

entries.position: both — the with sense usually follows a verb

entries.meaning: Without energy, care or interest in something that matters. ---
examples: The team's lackadaisical first half cost them the game.
He was let go for his lackadaisical attitude toward deadlines.
Nobody is more lackadaisical about answering email than my brother.

entries.meaning: Dull and without energy, excitement or quality. ---
examples: Sales have been lackluster since the spring.
Critics called the movie lackluster.
After a lackluster start, the band finally woke up.
entries.contrast: American spelling lackluster; the British form is lacklustre.

entries.meaning: Using very few words. ---
examples: His laconic reply was just: Fine.
The sheriff was a tall, laconic man who nodded a lot.
She gets more laconic the angrier she is.
entries.contrast: laconic describes a person or a remark that uses very few words, often dryly. A short text that simply says everything briefly is concise.

entries.meaning: Producing milk for a baby or a young animal. ---
examples: The drug is not recommended for pregnant or lactating women.
Lactating cows are milked twice a day.
The hospital has a quiet room for lactating mothers.
entries.position: attributive only — a lactating mother; after a verb it is the verb: She is lactating

entries.meaning: Made of lace, or as delicate and full of small holes as lace. ---
examples: She wore a lacy white blouse.
Frost made a lacy pattern on the window.
The second dress was even lacier than the first.

entries.meaning: Loaded or filled with a large amount of something. ---
examples: The table was laden with food.
A heavily laden truck crawled up the hill.
His speech was laden with clichés.
entries.position: both — before a noun it usually needs an adverb (a heavily laden truck); after a verb it takes with
entries.form: an old participle of lade, to load; also the second half of compounds: fat-laden, snow-laden

entries.meaning: Polite and graceful in the way people once expected a woman to be. ---
examples: She sat with her ankles crossed in a ladylike way.
Burping at the table is not very ladylike.
Her grandmother's idea of ladylike behavior died out long ago.
entries.contrast: The word now sounds old-fashioned, and not very ladylike is usually a criticism of a woman's behavior rather than a neutral description.

entries.meaning: Stuck in bed or at home because of illness or injury. ---
examples: He's been laid up with a bad back for two weeks.
I was laid up for a month after the surgery.
Half the team is laid up with the flu.
entries.position: predicative only — after be or get: He's laid up with the flu
entries.contrast: Do not confuse it with laid off, which means you lost your job because the company cut staff.

entries.meaning: Relaxed and not easily worried or made angry. ---
examples: Her dad is really laid-back about curfews.
It's a laid-back office — nobody wears a tie.
Portland felt more laid-back than New York.

entries.meaning: Having lost a job because the employer cut staff. ---
examples: The city set up a job fair for laid-off factory workers.
Laid-off employees keep their health coverage for three months.
A group of laid-off engineers started their own company.
entries.position: attributive only — after a verb it is the passive: She was laid off in May
entries.form: from the phrasal verb lay off
entries.contrast: laid-off means the job disappeared; fired means the person was let go for bad work or misconduct.

entries.meaning: Laissez-faire has 2 distinct senses.
examples: They argued for a laissez-faire approach to the internet.
The 1920s were a laissez-faire decade in American banking.
Her parents were laissez-faire about homework.
He has a more laissez-faire management style than his predecessor.

senses.head: Of a government or an economy: leaving business alone, with few rules
examples: They argued for a laissez-faire approach to the internet.
The 1920s were a laissez-faire decade in American banking.

senses.head: Of a person: leaving others to do as they like
examples: Her parents were laissez-faire about homework.
He has a more laissez-faire management style than his predecessor.

entries.meaning: Lame has 2 distinct senses.
examples: That's the lamest excuse I've ever heard.
The party was kind of lame.
He made a lame joke about my haircut.
The horse went lame after the third race.
One of the puppies is lame in a back leg.

senses.head: Informal: weak, unconvincing or boring
examples: That's the lamest excuse I've ever heard.
The party was kind of lame.
He made a lame joke about my haircut.

senses.head: Unable to walk normally because of an injured leg or foot
examples: The horse went lame after the third race.
One of the puppies is lame in a back leg.

entries.contrast: Used of a person, lame for unable to walk well now sounds offensive; people say has trouble walking or name the condition. The informal sense is the one you hear every day.

entries.meaning: Very bad or disappointing, in a way that deserves regret. ---
examples: The report describes a lamentable failure of oversight.
Her handwriting is lamentable.
It is lamentable that so few people voted.

entries.meaning: Surrounded by land, with no coast on the sea. ---
examples: Bolivia has been landlocked since 1884.
Landlocked countries pay more to ship their goods.
A dozen landlocked states depend on the river for trade.

entries.meaning: Planted and arranged to look attractive. ---
examples: The apartments have beautifully landscaped grounds.
A landscaped median runs down the middle of the boulevard.
The backyard is fully landscaped, so there is nothing left to do.

entries.meaning: Slow and relaxed, without energy, often in a pleasant way. ---
examples: They spent a languid afternoon by the pool.
She waved a languid hand at the waiter.
The music had a languid, sleepy rhythm.

entries.meaning: Tall and thin, with long arms and legs. ---
examples: A lanky teenager answered the door.
He's lanky like his father.
The lankiest kid on the team plays center.

entries.meaning: From Laos, or connected with Laos. ---
examples: We ate at a Laotian restaurant downtown.
Her grandparents are Laotian.
The museum has a room of Laotian textiles.
entries.contrast: Also a noun: a Laotian. The language is Lao, and Lao also works as the adjective.

entries.meaning: Lapsed has 2 distinct senses.
examples: He calls himself a lapsed Catholic.
A lapsed Baptist, she still knows every hymn by heart.
The company sent a notice about her lapsed policy.
You can restore a lapsed membership for a small fee.

senses.head: No longer practicing the religion you were raised in
examples: He calls himself a lapsed Catholic.
A lapsed Baptist, she still knows every hymn by heart.

senses.head: No longer valid because it was not renewed or paid for
examples: The company sent a notice about her lapsed policy.
You can restore a lapsed membership for a small fee.

entries.meaning: Of a company or its stock: with a very large total market value. ---
examples: The fund holds mostly large-cap stocks.
Large-cap companies fell less than the rest of the market.
He moved his savings into a large-cap index fund.

entries.meaning: Involving a lot of people, money, space or effort. ---
examples: The city is planning large-scale repairs to the water system.
Large-scale farming needs heavy machinery.
There has been no large-scale violence since the election.
entries.comparison: not gradable — though the compound larger-scale is common

entries.meaning: Larger-than-life has 2 distinct senses.
examples: Her father was a larger-than-life character who knew everyone in town.
The coach's personality is larger-than-life.
A larger-than-life statue of the founder stands in the lobby.
